summary: This note gives an overview of tuberculosis (TB), covering its global prevalence, infection and death figures, and regional and demographic disparities. It also discusses drugs being studied for multidrug-resistant TB, including bedaquiline and the safety concerns around it, and efforts to speed vaccine development, including a large Gates Foundation gift to the Aeras Global TB Vaccine Foundation.
one_line: Overview of tuberculosis: global infection and death statistics, regional and demographic disparities, drug-resistant TB treatments, and vaccine development efforts.
key_facts: Roughly one-third of the world's population is thought to be infected with TB.
New TB infections occur in about 1% of the population each year.
In 2014, there were 9.6 million cases of active TB, which resulted in 1.5 million deaths.
More than 95% of TB deaths occurred in developing countries.
In 2010, 8.8 million new cases of TB were diagnosed, and 1.20–1.45 million deaths occurred.
About 0.35 million of the 1.45 million TB deaths in 2010 occurred in people also infected with HIV.
In 2007, Swaziland had the highest estimated TB incidence rate, at 1,200 cases per 100,000 people.
In 2007, India had the largest total TB incidence, with an estimated 2.0 million new cases.
In the United States, racial and ethnic minorities accounted for 84% of all reported TB cases.
Bedaquiline received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval in late 2012.
Existing data suggest patients taking bedaquiline in addition to standard TB therapy are five times more likely to die than those without the new drug.
The Aeras Global TB Vaccine Foundation received a gift of more than $280 million (US) from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation.
The Aeras gift aims to develop and license an improved TB vaccine for use in high burden countries.
Researchers and policymakers are promoting new economic models of vaccine development, including prizes, tax incentives, and advance market commitments.
